t: Data, information and knowledge; quality of information; validation and verification
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson FD06: Data, information and knowledge; quality of information; validation and verification.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Use one real example to show how raw data becomes information and then knowledge. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Data is a collection of raw facts and figures, numbers, text, codes, dates, images or sounds, that has no context and therefore no meaning on its own. The sequence 11.2, 9.6, 12.4 could be anything. When data is processed and given context, for example by labelling it as the bleep-test levels of three under-16 rugby players, it becomes information, which has meaning for the person using it. This is often summarised as information equals data plus context plus meaning.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Knowledge goes one step further: it is produced by applying a rule, or a set of rules, to information so that an informed decision can be made. If the coach's rule is that any player below level 10 needs extra conditioning, then knowing that one particular player must join that group is knowledge. The distinction matters because organisations collect data in order to produce information, and they use information, together with their own rules and experience, to make decisions. In an answer, always show all three levels using the same example so that the progression from raw values, to meaningful information, to a decision based on a rule is clear.
Right. What else do we need to know?

The quality of information depends on the quality of the data used to produce it, an idea summed up as 'garbage in, garbage out' (GIGO). Errors creep in in several ways. A transcription error happens when data is mistyped, such as 1500 entered instead of 150. A transposition error happens when two characters swap places, such as 40719 becoming 47019.
Got it. Keep going.

Spreadsheets may contain incorrect formulae, which can be caught by calculating important totals in two different ways and comparing them. Surveys may produce biased or meaningless results if questions are poorly worded or only one group of people is asked. Good-quality information has six characteristics: it is accurate, relevant to the user and purpose, up to date, complete enough for the decision, well presented in a suitable format, and reliable because it comes from a trustworthy, verified source. Using poor information can be worse than having none, because people act on it with false confidence and may make costly or dangerous decisions.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Information is valuable to an organisation when it leads to better decisions, lower costs, better customer service or an advantage over competitors. A supermarket that knows which products sell on which days can order the right stock and reduce waste; a hospital that knows its bed occupancy can plan staff rotas. The value of information falls if it arrives too late to influence a decision, if it is inaccurate or incomplete, or if competitors have the same information.
Okay. Keep going.

Information also has a cost: collecting the data, entering and checking it, storing it securely, keeping it up to date and training staff to use it all cost money. An organisation should therefore only collect information whose value is greater than its cost. Where information is about identifiable people, it is personal data, and it must be processed lawfully, fairly and securely under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, which also requires that data is accurate, kept up to date and not held for longer than necessary.
Go on.

Validation is an automatic check made by software when data is entered, to confirm that the input obeys set rules and is reasonable and sensible. A range check makes sure a value lies between a lower and an upper limit, such as a shoe size from 1 to 15. A type check makes sure the data is of the correct type, such as an integer for a number of tickets. A length check makes sure the right number of characters has been entered, such as exactly 11 characters for a mobile number.
Right. Keep going.

A format check makes sure the data matches a pattern, such as two letters followed by four digits. A presence check makes sure a field has not been left blank, which is why online forms mark compulsory fields with an asterisk. A lookup check compares the entry with a list or file of valid values, such as checking that a membership number exists in the members file. Often several checks are needed on one field, because a format check alone would accept an impossible date such as 45/33/87.
Go on.

Verification checks that data has been entered or copied accurately, so that every copy exactly matches the original source. In double entry, the data is entered twice and the computer compares the two versions, flagging any difference; this is why websites ask you to type a new password or email address twice. Double entry catches most typing mistakes but doubles the workload, so for large volumes it is usually kept for the most important fields. In proofreading, or visual checking, the data on screen or on a printout is compared by eye with the source document.
Makes sense. Keep going.

It works best when a different person does the checking, as in a pharmacy where a second pharmacist checks the printed label against the prescription. Proofreading is slow and expensive for large amounts of data and errors can be overlooked when people rush. Many systems also display the entered details and ask the user to confirm them, and backup software verifies that the copy matches the original.
Go on.

Validation and verification reduce errors but cannot remove them completely. Validation only checks that data is reasonable, so a value that is sensible but wrong will be accepted: an age of 34 typed instead of 43 passes any sensible range check. Some impossible values can also slip through if the rules are too simple; a day-of-month check of 1 to 31 accepts 31 April. Verification only checks that the copy matches the source.
Got it. Keep going.

If the original paper form contains a mistake, or the customer gave the wrong information, then the stored data will be an exact copy of a wrong value. Double entry can be defeated when the person makes the same mistake twice, and proofreading depends on the concentration of the checker. Because of these limits, organisations combine methods: validation rules at the point of entry, verification of the most important fields, and processes for people to check and correct their own records, which is also a right under data protection law.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Data?
Raw facts and figures, such as numbers, text, images or sound, that have no context and therefore no meaning on their own.
Information?
Data that has been processed and given context so that it has meaning to the person using it.
Knowledge?
The result of applying one or more rules to information so that an informed decision can be made.
GIGO?
Garbage in, garbage out: if the input data is of poor quality, the output information will also be of poor quality.
Transposition error?
An input error in which two characters are entered in the wrong order, such as 47019 instead of 40719.
Transcription error?
An input error in which data is copied or typed incorrectly, such as 1500 instead of 150.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Questions on this lesson usually use State, Describe, Explain or Compare and carry one mark per valid point. For data, information and knowledge, mark schemes credit a definition plus an example for each, ideally taken from the table or scenario given: raw value, value with context, then a rule applied to reach a decision. Knowledge answers that do not mention applying a rule usually lose the mark. For quality factors, name the factor and explain its effect in the context, for example that an incomplete re-order message does not say which pack size to buy. For validation, name the check and give the precise rule with the field and limits, such as 'range check: hour greater than or equal to 0 and less than or equal to 23'. 'Checks the data is correct' is never credited for validation; say 'sensible' or 'reasonable'. For verification, describe how the method works and a drawback. Common mistakes are confusing a type check with a format check, describing double entry as validation, and claiming that either method guarantees accuracy.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Why would validation NOT detect that a customer's age has been typed as 34 instead of 43? Is it A, Validation only runs on text fields; B, Validation only checks data after it has been stored; C, 34 is still a sensible, reasonable age, so it passes the rules; D, Ages cannot be validated?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: 34 is still a sensible, reasonable age, so it passes the rules. Validation checks reasonableness against rules, not truth; both values are valid ages.
That's it for Data, information and knowledge; quality of information; validation and verification. Next, try the worksheet and the quiz for this lesson on the hub.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
